mekki-muskil:1-1.t:
His saying, the Exalted: (لا أقسم): (لا) is redundant (zāʾida), because it is in the status of one occurring in the middle [of speech], since the whole Qur'an was sent down at one time to the lowest heaven, and was then sent down upon the Prophet, upon him be peace, after that over twenty-odd years, as Allah willed, of what He wished to send down piece by piece. If a speaker were to begin speech, it would not be permissible for him to bring a redundant (لا) at the beginning of his speech. It is also said that (لا) is not redundant; it is only a rejection of speech that preceded in another sūra. The second (لا) is not redundant: Allah, exalted be His mention, informed us that He swore by the Day of Resurrection and that He did not swear by the self-reproaching soul. Whoever read (لأقسم) without an alif made it a lām of oath entering upon (أقسم); this is far-fetched because of the omission of the nūn, since it should properly be (لأقسمن). It was permissible with the omission here only because he made (أقسم) refer to the present; when it is present, the nūn is not obligatory in the oath, because the nūn is obligatory in most cases only to distinguish between the present and the future. It has also been said that it is for the future, but the nūn was omitted, just as they allowed omitting the lām of the oath while keeping the nūn; and they recited:
... وقتيل مرة أثأرن فإنه فرغ وإن أخاهم لم يثأر ...
(And the slain of Murra I will surely avenge, for his blood is unavenged, while their brother has not been avenged.)
Sībawayh allowed the omission of the nūn that accompanies the lām in the oath.

mekki-muskil:4-4.t: His saying (بلى قادرين): it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of an implied verb, its implied form being "Yes, We shall gather them, being able"; this is the view of Sībawayh. It is also said that (قادرين) is accusative because it occurs in the position of (نقدر), the implied form being "Yes, We are able"; when the noun was put in the place of the verb, it was made accusative. This is a view far from the correct one; it would entail the accusative of (قائم) in your saying "I passed by a standing man" (مررت برجل قائم), because it is in the position of (يقوم).

mekki-muskil:6-6.t: His saying (يسأل أيان يوم القيامة): (أيان) is an adverbial of time (ẓarf zamān) meaning "when", and it is indeclinable (mabnī). It should properly have been vowelless, but two vowelless letters met, the alif and the nūn, so the nūn was given fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, like (كيف) and (أين). Indeclinability was necessary for (أيان) only because it means (متى), so it contains the meaning of the interrogative and resembles the interrogative particle; so it was made indeclinable, since the basic state of particles is indeclinability.

mekki-muskil:9-9.t: His saying (وجمع الشمس والقمر): (جمع) came in the masculine form although (الشمس) is feminine only because it is construed according to the meaning, as if He said "the two lights were gathered" or "the two luminaries"; this is the view of al-Kisāʾī. It is also said: since the implied form is "it was gathered between (بين) the sun and the moon", the verb was made masculine for the masculinity of (بين). It is also said: since the meaning is "they were gathered together", as the statement is not complete except with the moon, and the moon is masculine, the masculine prevailed, according to the origin of putting the verb after both of them. Al-Mubarrad said: since the femininity of (الشمس) is not real, the masculine is permissible in it, since femininity in this kind does not occur to distinguish between one thing and another.

mekki-muskil:10-10.t:
His saying (أين المفر): (المفر) is a maṣdar (verbal noun), so it means "where is the fleeing?"
His saying (بل الإنسان على نفسه بصيرة): (الإنسان) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), (بصيرة) is a second mubtadaʾ, and (على نفسه) is the khabar (predicate) of (بصيرة); the clause is the khabar of (الإنسان). The precise sense of its implied form is: "Rather, over man there are watchers from himself against himself who bear witness against him." (بصيرة) may also be the khabar of (الإنسان), the hāʾ in (بصيرة) being for intensification. It is also said: since its meaning is "a proof against himself", it entered for the femininity of (الحجة) "proof".

mekki-muskil:22-22.t: His saying (وجوه يومئذ ناضرة): (وجوه) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), (ناضرة) is a naʿt (adjective) of it, and (إلى ربها ناظرة) is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ. (ناضرة) may also be the khabar and (إلى ربها ناظرة) a second khabar. (ناظرة) may also be a naʿt of (ناضرة) or of (وجوه), with (ناضرة) the khabar of (الوجوه). The entry of (إلى) with looking indicates that it is looking with the eye and not from waiting; had it been from waiting, (إلى) would not enter with it. Do you not see that you do not say "I waited to Zayd" (انتظرت إلى زيد), while you say "I looked at Zayd" (نظرت إلى زيد)? So (إلى) accompanies the looking of the eye and does not accompany the "looking" of waiting. Whoever said that (ناظرة) means "awaiting" has erred in meaning and in i'rab, and has put speech out of its place. Some of the Muʿtazila deviated at this place, and their arbitrariness and departure from the community reached the point that they said (إلى) is not a preposition but a noun, the singular of (آلاء) "favours", and (ربها) is genitive by the annexation of (إلى) to it, not by a preposition; the implied form according to him is "the favour of its Lord is awaited". This is impossible in meaning, because the Exalted said (وجوه يومئذ ناضرة), i.e. "radiant with bliss", and He has informed us that they are blissful, so bliss has entered upon them and its signs have appeared on them; how then would one await what Allah has told us is present in them? One awaits only a thing that does not exist; as for a thing that exists and is present, how is it awaited? Is it permissible for you to say "I am waiting for Zayd" while he is with you, has not left you, and his leaving you is not expected? This is great ignorance from the one who interprets it so. Some of the Muʿtazila held that (ناظرة) is from looking with the eye, but said that its meaning is "looking at the reward of their Lord"; this too is a departure from the apparent meaning. If this were permissible, then "I looked at Zayd" would be permissible in the sense of "I looked at Zayd's gift", and this is a breaking of the speech of the Arabs, and in it is confusion and breaking of meanings. Moreover, we say: if the matter were so, the greatest awaited reward would be looking at Him; there is no god but He.

mekki-muskil:31-31.t: His saying (فلا صدق ولا صلى): the second (لا) is negation and is not a conjunction; its meaning is "he did not believe and did not pray".

mekki-muskil:33-33.t:
His saying (يتمطى): in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in (ذهب). Its origin is (يتمطط), from (المطيطاء) "strutting", but they replaced the second ṭāʾ with a yāʾ, and it turned into an alif because it was vowelled and what precedes it had fatḥa. (التمطط) is stretching.
His saying (سدى): accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun in (يترك), and (أن) [with its clause] stands in place of the two objects of (حسب).

mekki-muskil:39-39.t: His saying (الذكر والأنثى): a badal (substitute) from (الزوجين). (جعل) means "created", which is why it passes to only one object.

mekki-muskil:40-40.t: His saying (أن يحيي الموتى): assimilation in the two yāʾs is not permissible according to the grammarians, just as it is not permissible when you do not put the verb in the accusative, because if you assimilated, two vowelless letters would meet, since the second is vowelless, and the first is not assimilated until it is made vowelless. Likewise, for every letter you assimilate into a letter after it, the first must be made vowelless. They agree on disallowing assimilation in the nominative state. As for the accusative state, al-Farrāʾ allowed it because of the vowel on the second yāʾ; but it is not permissible according to the Basrans, because the vowel is incidental, not original.
